claim: Indoor air is always cleaner than outdoor air
explanation: Indoor PM2.5 can exceed outdoor levels due to cooking, incense, poor ventilation, and lack of filtration. In well-sealed homes without purifiers, indoor levels typically reach 60-80% of outdoor levels.
source: US EPA Indoor Air Quality Guide

explanation: Surgical masks block about 40% of PM2.5 particles — better than nothing, but far less effective than a well-fitted N95 (which blocks about 76% accounting for fit). Cloth masks block roughly 20%.

claim: Houseplants can significantly purify indoor air
explanation: While plants do absorb some pollutants, studies show you would need hundreds of plants per room to match even a small air purifier. A single purifier with CADR 150 m³/h does more than 500 plants.
source: Cummings & Waring (2020), Journal of Exposure Science

claim: Opening windows during high pollution is never helpful
explanation: If indoor pollution from cooking or other sources exceeds outdoor levels, brief ventilation can actually reduce exposure. AirPlan calculates exactly when this window exists based on your hourly forecast.

AQI 100-150 ('Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups') can trigger symptoms in people with asthma, heart conditions, elderly individuals, and young children. These groups should limit prolonged outdoor exposure.

claim: Running an exhaust fan while cooking is enough
explanation: Exhaust fans help but may not be sufficient. Gas stove cooking can produce 300+ µg/h of PM2.5. An exhaust fan removes some, but a closed kitchen with a fan still accumulates pollution. Opening a window briefly after cooking helps more.
source: Indoor Air Quality Research, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory
